title: Geospatial Indexing
subtitle: Watch a ride app find the nearest drivers by turning 2D space into cells it can look up directly.
learn: Why latitude and longitude do not work well with ordinary indexes
How geohash turns a location into a string whose prefix means 'same box'
How a quadtree adapts to crowded and empty areas
What S2 and H3 cells add, and why you search a cell plus its neighbours
How a live driver index is kept fresh and queried in a few milliseconds

steps.title: Who is closest to me?
steps.body: A rider taps 'request ride' at one point in a city. About 200,000 drivers are online in the metro area, each one a latitude and longitude that changes every few seconds. The app must return the 5 closest available drivers in well under a second. How do you search positions without checking every driver?
steps.idea: Proximity search asks for everything near a point, and a point has two coordinates, not one.
steps.caption: A rider asks for nearby drivers.

steps.title: The naive scan
steps.body: The simplest answer computes the distance to every driver and sorts. That is 200,000 distance calculations per request. An ordinary B-tree index on latitude does not rescue you: it narrows one axis to a long horizontal stripe across the whole city, and you still filter the rest. Assume this scan costs roughly 400 ms from a database; that is an assumption, but it is far too slow at thousands of requests per second.
steps.idea: A one-dimensional index cannot answer a two-dimensional 'nearby' question efficiently.
steps.caption: Scanning every driver is slow.

steps.title: Geohash: space as a string
steps.body: Geohash repeatedly halves the map, alternating longitude and latitude, and writes the resulting bits as a short string such as 'tdr1v7'. Points in the same box share the same prefix. At 6 characters a cell is roughly 1.2 km by 0.6 km; at 7 it is about 150 m square. Now 'nearby' becomes an ordinary lookup: fetch the drivers stored under the rider's cell key.
steps.idea: Geohash turns a 2D position into a string key, so a plain key lookup or prefix scan finds a neighbourhood.
steps.caption: Look up one cell key, not every driver.

steps.title: The boundary problem
steps.body: A rider standing at the edge of a cell may have the closest driver just across the line, in the next cell with a completely different prefix. Close points can have different hashes, and similar prefixes can be far apart. The standard fix is to query the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbours, then compute exact distances on those few results.
steps.idea: Cells are a coarse filter: search the cell and its neighbours, then rank by exact distance.
steps.caption: Query 9 cells, get a short candidate list.

steps.title: Quadtree: cells that adapt
steps.body: A quadtree starts with the whole map as one box. Whenever a box holds more than a set number of points, say 100, it splits into four children, and so on. Dense downtown ends up in tiny boxes while an empty suburb stays one big box. Lookups descend the tree. The catch is that it usually lives in memory on one node, and moving drivers mean constant inserts and removals.
steps.idea: A quadtree splits only where data is dense, so every leaf holds a similar number of points.
steps.caption: Tree descends to a small leaf box.

steps.title: S2 and H3: cells on a sphere
steps.body: Flat grids distort near the poles and edges. Google's S2 maps the globe onto a cube and orders cells along a space-filling curve, so each cell is a single 64-bit id and nearby cells get nearby ids. Uber's H3 uses hexagons, whose 6 neighbours are all the same distance away, which makes 'rings' of cells simple. At H3 resolution 8, a hexagon is about 0.7 square km.
steps.idea: S2 and H3 are geohash's idea done on the sphere: fixed ids per cell, with cheap neighbour and ring lookups.
steps.caption: Search the rider's hexagon plus a ring.

steps.title: Keeping drivers fresh
steps.body: Each driver app sends a GPS ping every 4 seconds, so 200,000 drivers produce about 50,000 writes per second. Pings go onto a stream, and an updater reads them. It writes only when a driver crosses into a new cell: remove the id from the old cell's set, add it to the new one. Entries expire after a short TTL so drivers who go offline drop out on their own.
steps.idea: The index changes constantly, so write only on cell changes and let stale entries expire.
steps.caption: Pings flow in; cell moves update the index.

steps.title: Rank and answer
steps.body: With about 60 candidate ids in hand, the service loads each driver's current coordinates, rating, and availability from the driver store. It computes true distance, drops anyone who is busy or too far, sorts, and returns the top 5. The cell lookup shrank 200,000 drivers to a few dozen, so the expensive exact work runs on almost nothing.
steps.idea: Two phases win: a cheap cell filter to shortlist, then exact math on the shortlist.
steps.caption: Shortlist, exact distance, top 5 back.

steps.title: A stadium empties
steps.body: Fixed-size cells assume roughly even density. After a concert, 5,000 drivers and riders pile into a single cell, so one lookup returns a huge list while the quiet cell next door is empty. Fixes: use a finer resolution where cells are busy, let a quadtree split that area, or cap the shortlist and expand outward ring by ring only if you need more.
steps.idea: Uneven density breaks fixed cells; go finer or adaptive in hot spots.
steps.caption: One hot cell returns thousands of ids.

steps.title: From 200,000 to a few dozen
steps.body: Proximity search is hard because 'near' is two-dimensional. Geohash, quadtrees, S2, and H3 all map space to cells so that a lookup replaces a scan. Always search the cell plus its neighbours, then rank by exact distance. Keep the index in memory, update it only when a driver changes cell, and choose cell size to match how crowded the area is.
steps.idea: Index space as cells, shortlist by cell and neighbours, then rank exactly.
steps.caption: Cells turn a scan into a lookup.

quiz.q: Why can't a plain B-tree index on latitude alone make 'drivers within 2 km' fast?
options: B-trees cannot store decimal numbers
It narrows only one axis, leaving a long stripe of rows to filter by longitude
Latitude values are not sortable
It only works for exact matches
quiz.why: A latitude range selects a band across the whole city. The longitude condition still has to be checked row by row inside it, so the index helps far less than for a one-dimensional query.

quiz.q: A rider sits right on the edge of a geohash cell. What query avoids missing the closest driver?
options: Search only the rider's own cell with a longer prefix
Search the rider's cell and its 8 neighbours, then sort by exact distance
Sort all drivers by their geohash string
Retry with a shorter hash only if the first result is empty
quiz.why: Nearby points can fall in different cells. Reading the neighbours covers the boundary, and exact distance on the small shortlist picks the true closest.

quiz.q: Which situation most favours a quadtree over fixed-size cells?
options: Drivers spread evenly across a flat plain
A dense downtown next to large empty areas
Needing a 64-bit id per location
Storing the index only on disk
quiz.why: A quadtree splits only where points are dense, so crowded and empty regions both end up with a manageable number of points per leaf. Fixed cells waste work on empty areas or overflow in busy ones.

quiz.q: Drivers ping every 4 seconds, yet the index is written far less often than that. What makes this possible?
options: Pings are dropped at random
The index is written only when a driver moves into a different cell
Cells are recomputed once per hour
Riders update the index instead
quiz.why: Most pings keep the driver in the same cell, so the cell membership does not change. Writing only on cell changes, plus TTL expiry for stale entries, cuts index writes substantially.

quiz.q: After a concert, one cell returns 5,000 candidates and queries slow down. What is the most sensible response?
options: Use a coarser cell size everywhere
Use finer cells or an adaptive split in that hot area
Remove the neighbour lookup
Move the index to disk
quiz.why: The cell is too coarse for that density. A finer resolution or a quadtree split keeps the shortlist small where the crowd is, without changing quiet areas.

cheatsheet.def: String encoding of a location from interleaved lat/lon bits. Longer string means smaller box; a shared prefix means the same enclosing box.
Close points can sit in different cells. Query the cell plus its neighbours, then rank by exact distance.
Recursive 4-way split of the map, splitting a box only when it holds too many points. Adapts to uneven density.
Google's library: sphere mapped to a cube, cells ordered along a Hilbert curve, each cell a 64-bit id with 31 levels.
Uber's hexagonal grid with 16 resolutions. Every neighbour is equidistant, so ring and distance queries are simple.
Use cells as a cheap coarse filter to shortlist tens of candidates, then compute exact distance on just those.
Rule of thumb: pick a size that holds tens of results, not thousands. Go finer in dense areas, widen rings in sparse ones.
